Body HTML:
The best gas water heater for a home is the tank model that fits the existing vent, burns the fuel you have, and has a first-hour rating that covers your busiest hour of hot water use. Brand comes after those three. A heater with the wrong vent type can cost more to install than the heater itself, so compare models in the order below: vent type, fuel, first-hour rating, BTU input, efficiency (UEF), then size and features.

How to compare gas water heaters: the short checklist

  1. Vent type: the same as the heater you are replacing, unless you plan a vent change.
  2. Fuel: natural gas or propane, matched to your supply.
  3. First-hour rating (FHR): equal to or slightly above your peak-hour demand.
  4. BTU/h input: within what your gas line and meter can supply.
  5. UEF: the highest you can justify, compared within the same usage bin.
  6. Dimensions: height, diameter and clearances that fit the space.
  7. Local rules: low-NOx, seismic strapping, expansion tank and permit requirements.

Which vent type do you need?

Venting decides which models can be installed without rebuilding the flue. It is the first filter, before brand or capacity.

Vent typeHow it worksWhere it fits
AtmosphericExhaust rises by natural draft through a draft hood into a Type B vent or a lined chimney. Combustion air comes from the room.Replacing a heater on a vertical flue that is in good condition. No electrical supply needed for venting.
Powered damperAtmospheric venting with a damper that closes the flue between burner cycles.The same flue as atmospheric, with less standby heat lost up the vent. Needs power for the damper.
Power ventA blower pushes exhaust through plastic pipe, usually out a side wall. Combustion air comes from the room.No usable chimney nearby. Needs an electrical receptacle for the blower.
Direct ventSealed combustion. Air is drawn from outdoors and exhaust leaves through the same wall, without a blower.Closets and tight houses where room air should not be used. The heater must sit near an outside wall.
Power direct ventSealed combustion with a blower. Intake and exhaust are both piped outdoors.Sealed installations that need longer vent runs. Needs an electrical receptacle for the blower.

Replacing like with like is almost always the simplest job. Changing vent type means new vent pipe, new wall or roof penetrations and sometimes a new electrical circuit. Vent material, diameter and maximum length are set by each model's installation manual, not by a general rule.

Natural gas or propane?

Natural gas and propane models use different orifices and gas control settings. Buy the version built for your fuel. A heater can be converted only with the manufacturer's kit for that exact model, installed by a qualified technician, and many residential tanks have no approved kit. The fuel is printed on the rating plate and is part of the model number.

What first-hour rating do you need?

The first-hour rating is the number of gallons of hot water the heater can deliver in one hour, starting with a full hot tank. It is printed on the yellow EnergyGuide label. Tank size alone does not tell you this: two 50-gallon heaters with different burners have different first-hour ratings.

To estimate your peak-hour demand, list the hot water uses that happen in your busiest hour and add them up. The U.S. Department of Energy publishes a sizing worksheet on its Energy Saver site with an average number of gallons for each kind of use. Look for a first-hour rating at or just above your total. Our guide What Size Water Heater Do I Need? works through more examples.

How much BTU input is enough?

BTU/h input is the size of the burner. A higher input reheats the tank faster, which raises the first-hour rating without a larger tank. Under the U.S. Department of Energy rules for consumer water heaters, a gas storage water heater with an input above 75,000 BTU/h falls outside the residential class.

A larger burner needs more gas. Before choosing a high-input model, have your installer confirm that the gas pipe, the meter and the regulator can carry the heater's full input together with every other gas appliance in the house. An undersized gas line causes poor ignition and a burner that never reaches its rating.

How do you compare efficiency (UEF)?

Uniform Energy Factor (UEF) is the federal efficiency rating for water heaters. A higher number means more of the fuel's energy ends up in the water. Under the Department of Energy test procedure, UEF is measured in four draw patterns (very small, low, medium and high usage), and a rating is comparable only with other heaters tested in the same pattern. The pattern and the estimated yearly operating cost are both on the EnergyGuide label.

Standard atmospheric tanks sit at the lower end of the range. Powered damper, power vent and condensing designs rate higher because less heat escapes through the flue.

What else should you check before ordering?

  • Height and diameter. Short and tall versions of the same capacity exist for low ceilings and narrow closets. Measure the space, the doorway and the height of the existing vent connection.
  • Low-NOx requirements. Some air quality districts, mainly in California, require ultra-low-NOx burners. Check the local rule before ordering.
  • Relief valve location. The temperature and pressure (T&P) relief valve may be on the top or the side. Matching the old position simplifies the discharge piping.
  • Thermal expansion. Where the cold supply has a check valve, backflow preventer or pressure reducing valve, plumbing codes require thermal expansion control, usually a water heater expansion tank.
  • Installation parts. Ask your installer what to have on hand. A typical job uses a new gas connector and sediment trap, water heater connectors, a drain pan, seismic straps where required and a shut-off valve. See water heater gas supplies and shut-off valves and leak protection.

To compare capacities, inputs and vent types side by side, browse the residential gas tank water heaters collection.

When to call a professional

Installing a gas water heater involves gas piping, combustion air, venting and a T&P relief valve. Errors in any of them can cause a gas leak, carbon monoxide in the house or a scalding discharge. In most jurisdictions the work needs a permit and a licensed plumber or gas fitter. Hire a professional when:

  • You are replacing a gas water heater at all, unless your local code allows homeowner installation and you can have it inspected.
  • The vent type is changing, or the existing flue is corroded, undersized or shared with another appliance.
  • The new heater has a higher BTU input than the old one.
  • You smell gas. Leave the building first and call the gas utility from outside.

Never remove, plug or cap a T&P relief valve or its discharge pipe, and never operate a heater with the draft hood or vent disconnected.

Frequently asked questions

What is the most important spec when comparing gas water heaters?

Vent type, because it decides what can be installed without major work. After that, compare first-hour rating, BTU input and UEF.

Is a power vent water heater better than an atmospheric one?

Not by default. A power vent solves the problem of a missing or unusable chimney. It needs electricity, will not run in a power outage, and its blower makes some noise. Where a sound vertical flue exists, an atmospheric or powered damper model is the simpler replacement.

Does a higher BTU water heater use more gas?

It burns gas faster while firing but fires for less time to heat the same water. Yearly gas use depends mainly on how much hot water you use and on the heater's UEF.

Can a natural gas water heater run on propane?

Only with the manufacturer's conversion kit for that model, installed by a qualified technician. If no kit is listed, buy the propane model.

Navien vs Rinnai comes down to installation details more than brand. Both make condensing gas tankless water heaters rated up to about 199,000 BTU/h with efficiency ratings of 0.95 to 0.98 UEF, and both offer models with a built-in recirculation pump. The practical differences are venting options, how each brand handles recirculation, the non-condensing lines, and which brand your installer is trained on. This guide compares the two on the facts each manufacturer publishes. We sell Navien, so use the manufacturer documents linked from each product page to check anything that matters for your job.

Navien vs Rinnai at a glance

 NavienRinnai
Residential condensing lineNPE-2 series: NPE-S2 (standard) and NPE-A2 (ComfortFlow)SENSEI RX series: RX (standard) and RXP (with pump)
Published efficiency0.96 UEF (NPE-S2), 0.95 UEF (NPE-A2)Up to 0.98 UEF on the largest RX models
FuelNatural gas, field convertible to propaneNatural gas or propane
Built-in recirculationNPE-A2: pump plus buffer tankRXP: pump
Condensing vent materials2 in. or 3 in. PVC, CPVC, polypropylene or stainless, per the manualThe vent systems approved in the Rinnai installation manual for the model
Non-condensing lineNHW-A and NHW-S series, 0.81 UEFRE series (REP models include a pump)

Which models are you actually comparing?

Navien

  • NPE-S2: the standard condensing model, such as the NPE-240S2 (199,900 BTU/h).
  • NPE-A2: the same heater with ComfortFlow, a built-in recirculation pump and buffer tank, such as the NPE-240A2.
  • NHW-A and NHW-S: non-condensing lines rated 0.81 UEF. The NHW-AI is an indoor model with a built-in pump and buffer tank, and the NHW-SU installs indoors or outdoors.

Rinnai

  • SENSEI RX: the residential condensing line. Models with a P in the name (RXP) include a recirculation pump.
  • RE series: the non-condensing line. REP models include a pump.

For a closer look at the two Navien condensing versions, see Navien NPE-A2 vs NPE-S2.

Condensing or non-condensing: decide this first

This choice changes venting, drainage and efficiency more than the brand does.

 Condensing (NPE-2, SENSEI RX)Non-condensing (NHW, RE)
EfficiencyAbout 0.95 to 0.98 UEFAbout 0.81 UEF on the Navien NHW models
Exhaust temperatureLow enough for plastic vent pipe where the manual allows itHot: needs the manufacturer's concentric or stainless vent system
Condensate drainRequired. Many codes also call for a neutralizer.Not required at the heater
Typical useNew installs and tank-to-tankless conversionsLike-for-like replacement of a non-condensing unit, outdoor installs

More detail is in condensing vs non-condensing tankless water heaters.

How does the efficiency compare?

UEF (Uniform Energy Factor) is the U.S. Department of Energy rating for water heaters. Navien publishes 0.96 UEF for the NPE-S2 and 0.95 for the NPE-A2. Rinnai publishes 0.98 UEF for its largest RX models, such as the RX199i. A difference of two or three hundredths changes the yearly gas bill only slightly. Correct sizing, an adequate gas supply and regular descaling affect real performance more. Check the exact model in the manufacturer's specification sheet or the ENERGY STAR product list.

How does the venting compare?

Venting often decides the installation cost, so price both brands against your real vent route.

  • Navien NPE-2: Navien approves 2 in. and 3 in. venting. The maximum length depends on the diameter and the number of elbows, so take it from the current installation manual. Approved materials include PVC, CPVC, polypropylene and stainless steel.
  • Navien NHW: concentric vent. Confirm the size in the manual.
  • Rinnai SENSEI RX: the approved vent systems, diameters and maximum lengths are in the installation manual for the model.
  • Rinnai RE: concentric vent. Confirm the size in the manual.

Vent pipe from a tank water heater cannot be reused for either brand. If you are replacing an existing tankless unit of the same brand and type, the existing vent may be reusable only if the new model's manual approves that vent system.

How does recirculation compare?

Recirculation keeps hot water near the fixtures so the wait at the tap is shorter.

  • Navien ComfortFlow (NPE-A2, NHW-AI): a built-in pump and a small buffer tank. The buffer tank reduces the short burst of cool water that can occur when a tankless heater restarts between draws. The manual covers piping with a dedicated return line and without one.
  • Rinnai (RXP, REP): a built-in pump. Rinnai's RX literature describes a recirculation feature called Smart-Circ. See the manual for how it works and which models have it.

With either brand, a house without a dedicated return line needs a thermostatic crossover valve at the farthest fixture. That method sends some warm water into the cold line while it runs.

What matters more than the brand?

  • Sizing. Size by flow rate at your winter temperature rise, not by BTU alone. See what size tankless water heater you need.
  • Gas supply. A 199,000 BTU/h heater often needs more gas than the tank it replaces. The pipe, meter and regulator must be checked against the total connected load.
  • Water quality. Both brands require periodic descaling in hard water. Isolation valves from a tankless valve kit make that possible without cutting pipe.
  • Condensate. Condensing models need a drain and, where required, a condensate neutralizer.
  • Service. Ask which brand your installer stocks parts for and is trained to commission.

Which should you buy?

  • Navien NPE-A2: you want recirculation with a buffer tank built into the heater.
  • Navien NPE-S2: you want a condensing unit without recirculation and want the option of 2 in. venting within the limits in the manual.
  • Rinnai RX or RXP: you are replacing a Rinnai, your installer works mainly with Rinnai, or a specific RX model meets your efficiency target.
  • Non-condensing (Navien NHW or Rinnai RE): you are replacing a non-condensing unit, or the heater goes outdoors and a condensate drain is impractical.

Compare models in Navien tankless water heaters or the full tankless water heaters collection. For fault codes on an installed unit, see Navien tankless error codes.

When to call a professional

Installing or converting a gas tankless water heater is not a homeowner job in most jurisdictions. It involves gas piping, venting, a condensate drain, an electrical supply and combustion setup, and it usually needs a permit. Use a licensed installer for the installation, for any propane conversion, for gas pressure checks and for any work inside the sealed combustion chamber. If you smell gas, leave the building and call the gas utility from outside.

Frequently asked questions

Is Navien or Rinnai more efficient?

On paper, Rinnai's highest RX rating (0.98 UEF) is slightly above Navien's NPE-S2 (0.96 UEF). The difference in gas use is small.

Can both brands vent with PVC?

Navien approves PVC for the NPE-2 within the limits in its manual. For a Rinnai RX model, check the installation manual. Non-condensing models from either brand need the manufacturer's concentric or stainless vent.

Do I need a recirculation model?

Only if long pipe runs make you wait for hot water. In a compact house with short runs, a standard model is simpler and has fewer parts.

You can clean a furnace flame sensor, but you should not clean a furnace ignitor. A hot surface ignitor is a brittle ceramic element: rubbing it with sandpaper, steel wool or even bare fingers can crack it or shorten its life, so an ignitor is inspected, tested with a multimeter and replaced if it fails. The part that does need cleaning is the flame sensor, the metal rod that proves the burners are lit. This guide shows how to tell the two apart, how to clean a flame sensor, how to test an ignitor and how to choose a replacement.

Ignitor or flame sensor: which one is the problem?

Watch one heating cycle through the sight glass in the burner door. A hot surface ignition furnace follows this order: inducer fan starts, pressure switch closes, ignitor glows, gas valve opens, burners light, flame sensor proves the flame, blower starts.

What you seeLikely causeWhat to do
Burners light, then go out after a few secondsDirty or poorly grounded flame sensorClean the flame sensor
Ignitor never glowsCracked or open ignitor, or no voltage from the controlInspect and test the ignitor
Ignitor glows, burners never lightGas supply, gas valve or controlCheck that the gas shut-off is open, then call a technician
Spark but no flame (spark ignition)Electrode gap, ignition cable or groundCall a technician

Most furnace controls also flash a fault code on a status LED. Read the code against the chart on the furnace door before replacing any part.

How does the furnace know the burners are lit?

A flame conducts a very small electrical current, a few microamps, and conducts it better in one direction. The control applies a voltage to the flame sensor rod, and the current returns through the flame to the grounded burner. This is called flame rectification. If the control does not see that current within a few seconds of opening the gas valve, it closes the valve. An oxide film on the rod, a cracked insulator or a poor burner ground reduces the current until the control can no longer prove the flame.

Some appliances use a separate flame rod (remote sense). Others ignite and sense through the same element (local sense). That difference matters when you choose a replacement ignitor.

Before you start

  • Switch off power at the furnace service switch or the breaker. On most hot surface ignition furnaces the ignitor runs on 120 V.
  • Close the manual gas shut-off on the furnace supply line.
  • Let the burner area cool.
  • Photograph the wiring before disconnecting anything.
  • If you smell gas, do not operate any switch. Leave the building and call the gas utility from outside.

How to clean a furnace flame sensor

The flame sensor is a thin metal rod in a white porcelain insulator, mounted so its tip sits in the burner flame. It has one wire and is usually held by one hex-head screw. On many furnaces it is at the opposite end of the burner row from the ignitor.

  1. With power and gas off, pull the single wire off the sensor terminal.
  2. Remove the mounting screw and slide the sensor straight out.
  3. Rub the metal rod lightly with a fine non-woven abrasive pad or fine steel wool until the dull film is gone. Do not use coarse sandpaper or emery cloth, which scratches the rod and leaves grit.
  4. Wipe the rod with a clean, dry cloth. Do not clean the porcelain with abrasives.
  5. Inspect the porcelain for cracks and the rod for pitting or bending. Replace the sensor if you find any.
  6. Reinstall the sensor in the same position and reconnect the wire.
  7. Restore gas and power and run a full cycle. The burners should stay lit.

If the burners still drop out, the cause may be a loose burner ground, a weak or lifting flame, or reversed polarity on the power supply. Those need a technician with a meter that reads flame current. A sensor that fouls again within weeks points to a combustion problem.

Can you clean a furnace ignitor?

No abrasive cleaning. The element of a hot surface ignitor is silicon carbide or silicon nitride. Skin oil, scratches and small knocks create weak spots that fail when the element heats. If the ignitor is dusty, leave it alone or blow the dust off gently without touching the element. If it is cracked, chalky white in one spot or does not glow, replace it.

How to test a furnace ignitor

  1. With the power off, unplug the ignitor from its harness and remove its mounting screw. Hold it by the ceramic base only.
  2. Look for hairline cracks, white spots and burned leads. A cracked ignitor must be replaced even if it still glows.
  3. Set a multimeter to ohms and touch the probes to the two connector pins.
  4. A reading of OL (open circuit) means the element is broken.
  5. If you get a reading, compare it with the manufacturer's specification for that ignitor. Resistance differs between silicon carbide and silicon nitride and between part numbers, so a general figure is not reliable.

If the ignitor tests good but never glows, the control may not be sending voltage. Measuring live 120 V inside a furnace is a job for a qualified technician.

How to choose a replacement ignitor or flame sensor

  • Start with the OEM part number. It is on the old part or in the furnace parts list. Ignitors that look alike differ in voltage, lead length, connector and bracket.
  • Match the voltage. Never fit an ignitor rated for a different voltage than the original.
  • Match the sensing type. Some universal ignitors are listed for remote flame sense applications only and must not be used on local sense systems. Check the ignitor instructions before ordering.
  • Universal kits. When the original is unavailable, a universal 120 V ignitor such as the Resideo Q3200U1004/U Glowfly can be used where its cross-reference lists your OEM part.
  • Flame sensors. Match rod length, bend and bracket. One example is the Resideo Q354A1018/U flame sensor.

Silicon carbide is the older grey element and is the more fragile of the two. Silicon nitride is tougher. Either is correct if the voltage, mounting and sensing type match the appliance.

What if the ignitor and sensor are both good?

The ignition control runs the light-off sequence and holds the safety timings. If the ignitor and sensor test good and the furnace still will not light, the control or the gas valve may be at fault. Replacement modules such as the Resideo S8910U3000/U universal hot surface ignition module must match the original's trial-for-ignition time, prepurge and flame sensing type. The trial time is a safety limit set by the appliance manufacturer: a replacement must never have a longer trial than the original. Diagnosis and replacement of a module or gas valve is technician work. See how to choose a furnace gas valve for the selection steps.

When to call a professional

  • You smell gas, or see soot, scorch marks or flame rolling out of the burner compartment.
  • The burners still drop out after the flame sensor is cleaned or replaced.
  • The ignitor glows but the burners never light.
  • A new ignitor fails again after a short time, which can indicate a voltage or control fault.
  • The work involves a gas valve, an ignition module, gas pressure or flame current measurement.
  • The furnace locks out repeatedly. Do not keep resetting it, and never jumper a pressure switch, rollout switch or limit switch to make it run.

Parts for this job

Browse gas ignition components for ignitors, flame sensors and ignition modules, pilot, burner and ignition parts, and gas valves. Have the furnace model number and the number printed on the old part ready when you look for a match.

Frequently asked questions

How often should a flame sensor be cleaned?

It is normally checked and cleaned during yearly furnace maintenance.

Can I clean a flame sensor with sandpaper?

Avoid coarse sandpaper. Use a fine non-woven abrasive pad or fine steel wool, then wipe the rod clean.

Why does my furnace light and then shut off?

The most common cause is a dirty or poorly grounded flame sensor. Other causes are a weak flame, a cracked sensor insulator, reversed supply polarity or a failing control.

Furnace gas valve replacement starts with two questions: is the valve really the failed part, and which valve matches the furnace? A replacement must match the original on six points: ignition type, number of stages, opening characteristic, pipe size, gas type and outlet pressure, and coil voltage. The model number on the old valve gives most of them. Fitting the valve is gas work for a licensed technician. It requires a leak test and a manometer reading and is not a do-it-yourself job. This guide explains how to confirm the diagnosis and how to choose the right Honeywell or Resideo valve.

What does a furnace gas valve do?

A modern furnace gas valve is a combination gas control. One body contains:

  • A manual shut-off: the ON/OFF knob or switch on the valve.
  • Two automatic valves in series: opened by 24 V coils only when the ignition control calls for gas. Two seats give redundancy if one leaks.
  • A pressure regulator: holds the outlet (manifold) pressure steady. The natural gas valves linked in this guide ship set at 3.5 in. WC, but the correct value is the one on the furnace rating plate.

The valve does not decide when to open. The thermostat calls for heat, the control runs the inducer and proves the pressure switch, the ignitor heats or sparks, and only then does the control power the valve. If flame is not proved within the trial period, the control closes it again.

How do you know the gas valve is bad?

The gas valve fails less often than the parts around it. Rule these out first:

  1. Thermostat and power. Confirm a call for heat, the furnace switch on and the door switch closed. A blank thermostat screen can look like a furnace fault.
  2. Fault code. Read the LED flash code on the control board against the chart on the door.
  3. Ignition. If the ignitor never glows or sparks, see how to test a furnace ignitor and clean a flame sensor.
  4. Flame that drops out. Burners that light and go out after a few seconds point to the flame sensor, not the valve.
  5. Gas supply. Check that the appliance shut-off and the valve's own knob are in the ON position.

The valve becomes the suspect when the furnace reaches the ignition step, the ignitor is hot or sparking, 24 VAC is present at the valve terminals during the trial, gas is available at the inlet, and still no gas reaches the burners. A technician confirms this with a multimeter and a manometer. Other signs are a regulator that will not hold the rated manifold pressure and a valve that does not close when the call ends.

If the burners stay lit after the thermostat is satisfied, close the manual gas shut-off and call a technician immediately.

How to choose the right replacement gas valve

Write down the full model number from the old valve label, for example VR8205A2024, and match the six points below. The furnace manufacturer's parts list is the final authority.

1. Ignition type

Ignition systemHow it lightsHoneywell/Resideo valve families
Standing pilotA pilot burns continuously and a thermocouple proves itVR8200, VR8300
Intermittent pilotA spark lights a pilot on each call, then the main valve opensVR8204, VR8304
Direct ignitionA hot surface ignitor or spark lights the main burner directlyVR8205, VR8215, VR8305
Universal electronic ignitionBuilt for both intermittent pilot and direct ignition appliancesVR8245, VR8345

Example: the Resideo VR8205A2024/U is a direct ignition valve. SmartValve (SV95xx) controls combine the gas valve and ignition control in one unit and are replaced only with the SmartValve specified for the appliance.

2. Single-stage or two-stage

A two-stage furnace needs a two-stage valve, which has a low and a high outlet pressure setting. A single-stage valve on a two-stage furnace gives no low fire.

3. Opening characteristic

Standard opening valves open fully at once. Slow opening valves ramp up for a softer light-off. Step opening valves open to a low rate first, then to full rate. Replace like with like unless the furnace manufacturer approves another type, because the opening characteristic affects ignition.

4. Pipe size and orientation

Match the inlet and outlet pipe size of the old valve. The valves linked in this guide are 1/2 in. x 1/2 in. Note whether the inlet and outlet are straight or use angle flanges.

5. Gas type and pressure

Valves ship set for natural gas or LP, and the regulator spring differs between the two. Conversion uses only the manufacturer's kit listed for that exact valve and opening type. A fuel conversion also means changing burner orifices and is work for a licensed technician.

6. Voltage

Most furnaces use 24 VAC valves. Line voltage (120 V) valves are a different design and are not interchangeable.

Is a Honeywell valve the same as a Resideo valve?

Yes, when the model number matches. Resideo makes the residential gas controls formerly sold under the Honeywell name and kept the model numbers. If the old label reads Honeywell VR8205A2024, the Resideo VR8205A2024/U is the same control in trade packaging.

Can a universal gas valve replace the original?

Often. Universal electronic ignition valves such as the 1/2 in. Resideo VR8245M2530/U are built to serve intermittent pilot and direct ignition appliances. Before substituting, confirm pipe size, stages, opening characteristic, gas type, capacity in BTU/h and that the valve's cross-reference lists the original part. The VR8205 is not a universal valve: it is for direct ignition only.

What does a correct replacement involve?

Replacing a gas valve is not a homeowner repair, and this guide does not give installation steps. Knowing what a proper job includes helps you check the work you are paying for. A licensed technician will:

  • Shut off the gas and the power before opening the gas train.
  • Install the valve the furnace manufacturer lists, with any fuel conversion kit the appliance requires.
  • Leak test every joint that was disturbed. Never with a flame.
  • Measure the inlet and manifold pressure with a manometer and set them to the rating plate.
  • Run several full cycles and check for smooth ignition, a stable flame and a clean shut-off.

When to call a professional

For this job, always. Gas valve replacement is regulated gas work in most jurisdictions and may need a permit, and it is not complete without a leak test and a manometer reading at the manifold. Use this guide to identify the right part, and have a licensed HVAC technician or gas fitter install it. Call one without delay when:

  • You smell gas. Leave the building and call the gas utility from outside.
  • The burners do not shut off, or light with a bang or delayed ignition.
  • The valve needs a fuel conversion or a pressure adjustment.
  • The checks above point to the gas valve or the ignition control.

Never tap, heat or force a gas valve open, and never bypass the ignition control to power a valve directly.

Parts for this job

Browse gas valves, gas ignition components and thermocouples and thermopiles, or all Resideo controls. Water heaters use a different control with a built-in thermostat; for those, see the water heater thermocouple guide.

A Honeywell thermostat with a blank screen has lost power. On battery models the cause is almost always dead batteries. On hardwired models the 24 VAC supply from the furnace or air handler has been interrupted, most often by a tripped breaker, a furnace door that is not fully closed, a blown fuse on the control board or a tripped condensate float switch. Work through the checks below in order, from the simplest to the ones that need a multimeter. They apply to Honeywell Home thermostats made by Resideo, including the PRO, FocusPRO and T-series.

Honeywell thermostat blank screen: quick checks

  1. Replace the batteries with fresh alkaline cells.
  2. Check that the thermostat is fully seated on its wallplate.
  3. Check the furnace or air handler breaker and the service switch.
  4. Close the furnace blower door firmly.
  5. Check the low-voltage fuse on the furnace control board.
  6. Look for water in the condensate pan or a tripped float switch.
  7. Check the R and C wires, then measure for 24 VAC.
  8. Restart the thermostat. If it has power and stays blank, replace it.

How is your thermostat powered?

Power typeTypical modelsWhere to look first
Batteries onlyBasic non-programmable and programmable models wired without a C wireBatteries, battery contacts
Batteries or 24 VAC (C wire)Many PRO, FocusPRO and T-series modelsBatteries first, then the 24 VAC supply
24 VAC only (C wire required)Wi-Fi models such as the T6 Pro Smart TH6220WF2006/UThe 24 VAC supply at the furnace or air handler

If you are not sure, pull the thermostat straight off its wallplate. Look for a battery compartment and check whether a wire is connected to the terminal marked C.

Step 1: Replace the batteries

Replace all the batteries with new alkaline cells of the size marked in the compartment, check the polarity, and clean any corrosion from the contacts. Snap the thermostat back onto the wallplate until it clicks. Most models show a low battery warning well before the display goes blank, so a screen that went dark without warning points to the HVAC power supply.

Step 2: Check the breaker and the furnace switch

A hardwired thermostat is powered by a transformer inside the furnace or air handler. If that equipment has no power, the screen is blank.

  • Reset the furnace or air handler breaker once if it has tripped. If it trips again, stop and call a technician.
  • Find the service switch on or near the furnace. It looks like a light switch and is easily turned off by mistake.
  • In a heat pump or air conditioning system, the indoor air handler has its own breaker, separate from the outdoor unit. The thermostat is powered from the indoor unit.

Step 3: Close the furnace door

Furnaces have a door safety switch that cuts power when the blower door is removed. If the door was not seated properly after a filter change, the switch stays open, the transformer has no power and the thermostat goes blank. Refit the door so it presses the switch fully. Do not tape or wedge the switch closed.

Step 4: Check the fuse on the control board

Most furnace and air handler control boards carry an automotive-style blade fuse that protects the 24 V circuit. It blows when two thermostat wires touch or a wire shorts to the cabinet, which often happens during a thermostat change.

  1. Turn off power to the furnace at the service switch or breaker.
  2. Remove the door and find the fuse on the control board.
  3. Pull the fuse and look at the metal link. A broken link means it has blown.
  4. Replace it only with a fuse of the same amp rating printed on the board. Never fit a larger fuse or bridge the holder.
  5. Before restoring power, look for the cause: bare wire touching metal, a pinched cable, stray strands at the thermostat, or damaged wire at the outdoor unit.

If the new fuse blows again, there is a short in the low-voltage wiring or a failed component. That needs a technician.

Step 5: Check the condensate float switch

Air conditioners, heat pumps and condensing furnaces produce condensate. Many systems have a float switch in the drain pan, drain line or condensate pump that shuts the system down when water backs up. On many installations the switch is wired in series with the R wire, so a full pan removes power from the thermostat. If you find standing water, clear the drain line, empty the pan and let the switch reset. Do not bypass the switch: it is there to prevent water damage. A drain that keeps clogging needs service.

Step 6: Check the wiring and measure the voltage

  • At the thermostat, each wire should be tight in its terminal with no bare copper touching a neighbor.
  • At the control board, the R and C connections should be tight.
  • With a multimeter set to AC volts, measure between R and C at the wallplate. A healthy system reads about 24 VAC. A slightly higher reading is normal.

No voltage with the breaker on, the door closed and a good fuse means a broken wire or a failed transformer. If a Wi-Fi thermostat has no C wire at all, it needs one. Our thermostat C-wire guide covers the options, including an adapter such as the Honeywell Home THP9045A1023/U WireSaver, which is installed at the equipment.

Step 7: Restart the thermostat

If power is confirmed and the screen is still blank or frozen, pull the thermostat off the wallplate, remove the batteries, wait a minute, then refit the batteries and the thermostat. Model-specific resets, including factory resets on T-series and Wi-Fi models, are in how to reset a Honeywell thermostat. A factory reset erases installer settings such as system type, so record them first.

When should you replace the thermostat?

Replace it when it has fresh batteries or a confirmed 24 VAC between R and C and the display still does not come on after a restart, or when the display is cracked or there is corrosion or water damage inside. Match the replacement to the system: number of heating and cooling stages, conventional or heat pump, and whether a C wire is present.

  • Honeywell PRO series thermostats, non-programmable, programmable and smart thermostats.

For the installation itself, follow the thermostat wiring guide.

When to call a professional

  • The breaker or the control board fuse trips or blows a second time.
  • There is no 24 VAC between R and C and the cause is not the door, fuse or float switch. Transformer and control board replacement involves 120 V or 240 V wiring.
  • The thermostat is a line voltage model (120 V or 240 V, used with electric baseboard heat). Those are not covered here and need an electrician.
  • You see burned wiring, a scorched control board or water inside the furnace.
  • You smell gas. Leave the building and call the gas utility from outside.

Always switch off power to the furnace or air handler before opening it. Thermostat wiring is 24 V, but the equipment it connects to is not.

Frequently asked questions

Why is my Honeywell thermostat blank after changing the batteries?

Check battery polarity and that the thermostat is fully snapped onto the wallplate. If the model is hardwired, the fault is in the 24 VAC supply: breaker, service switch, door switch, fuse or float switch.

Why did the screen go blank after I installed a new thermostat?

The usual cause is a blown low-voltage fuse on the furnace control board from wires touching during installation. The other is a missing C wire on a model that requires one.

Can a clogged AC drain make the thermostat go blank?

Yes, where the float switch interrupts the R wire. Clear the drain and the pan and the switch resets.

Does a blank screen mean the thermostat is broken?

Usually not. Replace the thermostat only after confirming that it has power.

Body HTML:
An aquastat is a switch that senses water temperature and uses it to control a boiler. Its sensing bulb sits in the boiler water, usually inside an immersion well, and its contacts turn the burner off at a high limit, keep the water above a low limit, or hold the circulator off until the water is hot. On most hot water boilers it is the gray box on the jacket with a temperature dial inside. This guide explains what an aquastat does, the main types, typical settings and how to choose a replacement.

What does an aquastat do on a boiler?

Depending on the model, an aquastat performs one, two or three functions:

  • High limit: opens the burner circuit when the boiler water reaches the set temperature. This is the operating limit that keeps the boiler from overheating during a long call for heat.
  • Low limit: fires the burner to keep the boiler at a minimum temperature when no thermostat is calling. It is used on boilers with a tankless coil for domestic hot water.
  • Circulator control: stops the circulator when the boiler water falls below the low limit, so the heat goes to domestic hot water first.

A room thermostat senses air and asks for heat. The aquastat senses water and decides whether the burner may fire and the circulator may run.

What is the differential?

The differential is the temperature change between the switch opening and closing again. For example, with a high limit set at 180°F and a 15°F differential, the burner shuts off at 180°F and can fire again when the water falls to about 165°F. A wider differential gives longer, less frequent burner cycles. Some controls have a fixed differential and others are adjustable.

What are the types of aquastats?

TypeWhat it doesResideo (Honeywell) examples
Single-function immersionOne switch, one setting: a high limit or a circulator controlL4006A, L4006B, L6006A
Manual reset high limitBackup limit that locks the burner out until a button is pressedL4006E, L4008E
Strap-on (surface mount)Clamps to a pipe instead of using a wellL6006C
Aquastat relayHigh limit plus a relay that runs burner and circulator from a 24 V thermostatL8148A, L8148E
Triple aquastat relayHigh limit, low limit and circulator control in one caseL8124A
Electronic aquastatThe same functions with an electronic sensor and LED displayL7224U

Single-function aquastats (L4006, L6006)

Two terms on the label describe the switch action. Breaks on rise means the contacts open as temperature rises, which is how a high limit works. The Resideo L4006A1017/U breaks on rise, with a 100 to 240°F range and a 5 to 30°F adjustable differential. Makes on rise means the contacts close as temperature rises, used to start a circulator only when the water is hot. L6006 models have SPDT contacts and can be wired for either action.

Manual reset high limits (L4006E)

A manual reset aquastat is a safety backup. If the water reaches its setting, it opens the burner circuit and stays open until someone presses the reset button. The Resideo L4006E1000/U has a 130 to 270°F range and is supplied with a 1/2 in. well. A manual reset limit that trips means the boiler overheated. Find the cause before the boiler goes back into service.

Aquastat relays (L8148)

An aquastat relay combines a high limit with a transformer and relay. The room thermostat connects to the T T terminals, and the control's relay switches the burner circuit and the circulator. The L8148A1017/U has a 140 to 240°F range with a fixed 8°F differential, and the L8148E1265/U has a 180 to 240°F range with a fixed 15°F differential. These are common on gas boilers.

Triple aquastats (L8124) and electronic aquastats (L7224U)

A triple aquastat adds a low limit to the high limit and circulator functions. It is the usual control on an oil boiler with a tankless coil, which stays hot all year. Resideo's L8124 family is the common example. The Resideo L7224U1002/U is a universal electronic replacement for oil boiler aquastats with high limit, low limit and circulator functions and an LED display.

What should a boiler aquastat be set to?

Use the settings in the boiler manufacturer's manual. As general guidance:

  • High limit: fin-tube baseboard and radiators are designed for hotter water than radiant floors. Do not set the limit above the boiler's rated maximum. Radiant floors need much cooler water and get it from a mixing device, not from turning the boiler limit down. See the mixing valve guide.
  • Low limit: on a triple aquastat, Honeywell's instructions call for the high limit to be set at least 20°F above the low limit. A boiler without a tankless coil may not need a low limit at all; ask a technician whether it applies to your boiler, because some cast iron boilers have a minimum return water temperature.
  • Differential: a larger differential reduces short cycling.

The aquastat high limit is not the only protection. The boiler also has a pressure relief valve, and many have a separate manual reset limit or low water cutoff. None of these should be disconnected or set beyond the boiler's ratings.

Boiler will not fire: is it the aquastat?

  1. Power and thermostat. Check that the service switch is on, the breaker is closed and the thermostat is calling for heat.
  2. Manual reset. Look for a tripped reset button on a manual reset limit or, on an oil burner, on the primary control. Press it once only. If it trips again, stop and call a technician. Repeated resets on an oil burner can flood the chamber with unburned oil.
  3. Settings. A high limit set below the current water temperature keeps the burner off.
  4. Burner fires but the radiators are cold. Look at the circulator and at air in the system instead. See choosing a boiler circulator and how to bleed a radiator.

Testing the relay, transformer and contacts means working on live 120 V terminals and is technician work.

How do you choose a replacement aquastat?

Match the control being removed, using its full model number:

  • Function: single limit, aquastat relay, triple or electronic.
  • Switch action: breaks on rise, makes on rise or SPDT.
  • Range and differential: the same or wider range, and a fixed or adjustable differential as on the original.
  • Reset: automatic or manual. Never replace a manual reset limit with an automatic one.
  • Mounting: immersion well, strap-on or remote bulb. If the old well stays, check its thread size and insertion length. Replacement wells include the Resideo 121371A/U (1/2 in. NPT, 3 in. insertion). Changing a well means draining the boiler below that tapping.
  • Thermostat circuit: 24 V, millivolt or line voltage.

Coat the sensing bulb with heat conductive grease where the control's instructions call for it, so the bulb reads the water temperature accurately. Browse all aquastats and wells.

When to call a professional

  • Replacing an aquastat or aquastat relay. These controls switch 120 V and are part of the boiler's safety chain, and a wiring error can leave the burner without a working limit.
  • A manual reset limit or burner primary control that trips more than once.
  • A relief valve that discharges, or boiler water that is hotter than the limit setting.
  • Any change of control type, for example fitting a triple aquastat where a relay was used.

Before removing any cover, turn off the boiler service switch and confirm the power is off. Never jumper a limit control to get a boiler running.

Frequently asked questions

What is the difference between an aquastat and a thermostat?

A thermostat senses room air temperature and calls for heat. An aquastat senses boiler water temperature and controls the burner and circulator.

Can I replace an L8148 with an L8124?

Not directly. They have different functions and wiring. Replace with the same type unless a technician confirms the system needs a low limit.

Body HTML:
A combi boiler (combination boiler) is a single gas appliance that heats a home through a hot water heating system and also heats domestic hot water on demand, with no storage tank. It replaces a separate boiler and water heater with one wall-hung unit. A combi suits homes with radiators, baseboard or radiant floors and moderate hot water use. It is not the right choice where several showers run at once or where the home is heated by forced air.

How does a combi boiler work?

One cabinet holds a gas burner, a primary heat exchanger, a circulator, a three-way (diverter) valve, a plate heat exchanger for domestic water and the controls. The boiler works in one of two modes:

  1. Space heating. A thermostat calls for heat. The burner fires and the pump sends heated boiler water around the radiators, baseboard or floor loops. The burner modulates its output to match the load.
  2. Domestic hot water. A hot tap opens and a flow sensor detects it. The three-way valve diverts boiler water through the plate heat exchanger, where it heats the cold water passing through the other side. The burner goes to the output needed for that flow.

Domestic hot water has priority. While a tap is running, the heating circuit gets no heat. In a correctly sized system this is rarely noticed, because radiators and floors hold heat for the length of a shower. The boiler water and the tap water never mix.

Combi boiler vs boiler with a tank vs tankless water heater

 Combi boilerBoiler + indirect tankTankless water heater
Space heatingYes, hydronicYes, hydronicNo
Domestic hot waterOn demand, limited by flow rateStored, with a reserve for peaksOn demand, limited by flow rate
Simultaneous heat and hot waterNo, hot water has priorityUsually priority as well, but the tank covers the drawNot applicable
Space neededOne wall-hung unitBoiler plus a floor-standing tankOne wall-hung unit
Fits bestHydronic homes with one or two bathroomsLarger homes, high peak demand, hard waterHomes heated by a furnace or heat pump

If the house has forced air heat, a tankless water heater is the matching product, and how a tankless water heater works explains the domestic side. If the house has a boiler, the choice is between a combi and a heating boiler with an indirect water heater.

What size combi boiler do you need?

A combi has two ratings and both must fit. Most sizing errors come from checking only one.

Heating: BTU/h against the heat loss

The heating output should match the home's design heat loss from a room-by-room calculation such as ACCA Manual J. The rating plate of the old boiler is not a reliable guide, because many older boilers were oversized. The minimum firing rate matters as much as the maximum: a low minimum lets the boiler run long, steady cycles in mild weather. The Navien NCB-240/130H, for example, lists a heating input range of 13,000 to 130,000 BTU/h, and the IBC CX199 has a 10:1 turndown from 199,000 BTU/h.

Hot water: GPM at your temperature rise

The domestic side is rated in gallons per minute (GPM) at a stated temperature rise. Temperature rise is the hot water setpoint minus the incoming cold water temperature: 120°F minus 50°F is a 70°F rise. The relationship is:

GPM = BTU/h output ÷ (500 × temperature rise in °F)

Navien lists the NCB-240/130H at 5.1 GPM at a 70°F rise from a 199,900 BTU/h domestic input. Add up the fixtures that run at the same time and compare. The flow rate is marked on most showerheads and faucets. In cold climates the winter rise is larger, so the same boiler delivers fewer gallons per minute.

When is a combi boiler a good fit?

  • The home has hydronic heat and one or two bathrooms, and rarely runs more than two hot fixtures at once.
  • Mechanical room space is limited.
  • The heat loss is moderate and falls inside the boiler's modulation range.

When is a boiler with an indirect tank the better choice?

  • Several showers, a large soaking tub or a multi-head shower run at the same time.
  • The incoming water is very cold or very hard. Hard water scales a plate heat exchanger.
  • The heating load is large and you want to size the boiler to the heat loss alone.
  • You want domestic hot water recirculation, which a storage tank handles more simply.

For that route, see condensing boilers and indirect water heaters.

What does a combi boiler installation need?

  • Venting. Condensing combis produce cool, acidic flue gas and vent through PVC, CPVC, polypropylene or stainless steel, never into an unlined masonry chimney. The approved materials, diameters and maximum lengths are specific to each model, and each elbow reduces the allowed length.
  • Condensate drain. The condensate is acidic and must run to a drain, through a condensate neutralizer where the manual or local code requires one.
  • Gas supply. A combi fires at a much higher rate for hot water than for heating (199,900 BTU/h on the NCB-240/130H), often well above the input of the boiler it replaces. The gas pipe, meter and regulator must be sized for the total connected load and pipe length. An undersized line causes ignition faults and poor hot water output.
  • Hydronic components. The heating loop is closed and pressurized. It needs a pressure relief valve, a fill valve with backflow protection, air removal and expansion capacity. Some combis have an internal expansion vessel that is too small for a large system, so an external heating expansion tank may be required.
  • Service valves. Isolation valves on the domestic side allow the plate heat exchanger to be descaled.

What maintenance does a combi boiler need?

  • Check system pressure on the gauge or display with the system cold and compare it with the manual's range. Frequent pressure loss means a leak. See how to bleed a radiator and fix high boiler pressure.
  • Descale the domestic heat exchanger on the schedule in the manual, more often in hard water.
  • Clean the filters on the cold water inlet and the heating return.
  • Keep the condensate trap clean and the vent and intake terminals clear of debris and snow.
  • Yearly professional service: burner inspection, combustion analysis, relief valve check and expansion tank pre-charge.

When to call a professional

Installing a combi boiler is licensed work: it combines gas piping, venting, condensate, hydronic piping, potable water and electrical connections, and it needs a permit in most jurisdictions. A combustion analysis at startup is the only way to confirm the boiler is burning safely. Also call a professional when:

  • The relief valve discharges or the pressure climbs toward its setting. Never plug or cap a relief valve.
  • The boiler shows repeated ignition or flame loss codes.
  • You smell gas or flue gas. Leave the building and call the gas utility from outside.
  • Any work is needed inside the sealed combustion chamber or on the gas valve.

Homeowner tasks are limited to checking the pressure, keeping terminals clear and cleaning the filters the manual describes as user-serviceable.

Compare combi boilers

Browse combination heating and DHW boilers and Navien combi boilers, and confirm the final selection against the manufacturer's sizing tables with your installer.

Frequently asked questions

Is a combi boiler the same as a tankless water heater?

No. Both heat water on demand, but a combi also runs a hydronic heating system. A tankless water heater makes domestic hot water only.

Can a combi boiler run two showers at once?

Yes, if its GPM at your winter temperature rise covers both showerheads. For example, two 2.0 GPM showerheads need about 4 GPM of mixed water, slightly less from the boiler.

Does a combi boiler need an expansion tank?

The heating loop always needs expansion capacity. Check whether the model has an internal vessel and whether it is large enough for the system volume.

To drain and flush a water heater, turn off the gas or the electricity, close the cold water supply, connect a garden hose to the drain valve, open a hot faucet, drain the tank, then flush it with short bursts of cold water until the water runs clear. Refill the tank completely before turning the power or gas back on. On a standard gas or electric tank water heater, flushing removes the sediment that causes rumbling noises and slow recovery.

How to drain and flush a water heater: the short version

  1. Turn off the power (electric) or set the gas control to off or pilot (gas).
  2. Close the cold water supply valve to the heater.
  3. Connect a hose to the drain valve and run it to a drain or outdoors.
  4. Open a hot water faucet in the house.
  5. Open the drain valve and let the tank empty.
  6. Flush with bursts of cold water until the water runs clear.
  7. Close the drain valve and refill the tank with the hot faucet open.
  8. When water flows steadily from the faucet, restore power or gas.

Why flush a water heater, and how often?

Minerals in the water, mostly calcium and magnesium, settle on the bottom of the tank. On a gas heater the layer sits between the burner and the water, which causes popping or rumbling and slows recovery. On an electric heater it can bury the lower element. Most manufacturers' manuals call for draining and flushing at regular intervals, more often with hard water. Follow the interval in your heater's manual.

Signs that a flush is overdue: popping or rumbling while the heater runs, hot water that runs out sooner than it used to, or gritty water from the drain valve.

Should you flush an old water heater that has never been flushed?

Be cautious. On an old tank with heavy buildup, sediment can block the drain valve so that it will not close again, and disturbing the sediment can expose a tank that was already corroded. If the heater is near the end of its life, shows rust at the base or already weeps water, plan a replacement instead of a flush.

What you need

  • A garden hose that reaches a floor drain, a laundry sink or outdoors, to a point lower than the drain valve
  • A flat screwdriver or pliers, for drain valves with a slotted stem
  • Gloves and safety glasses
  • A non-contact voltage tester, for electric heaters

Safety before you start

  • Scalding. Water in the tank is hot enough to scald. Shut the heater off and let the water cool for a few hours, or run hot water at a faucet until it cools, before draining. Make sure the hose end is secured and that the drain can accept hot water.
  • Electric heaters. Switch off the breaker, not only the thermostat. Most residential electric water heaters run on 240 V. Confirm the power is off with a voltage tester before removing any cover.
  • Gas heaters. If you smell gas, stop, leave the building and call the gas utility from outside.

Step 1: Turn off the power or the gas

Electric: switch off the water heater breaker. This is the most important step in the job, for the reason given in Step 7.

Gas: turn the gas control knob to OFF, or to PILOT or VACATION if your heater's manual allows that setting for draining. The burner must not fire while the tank is empty. If the heater has a power vent blower or an electronic control, unplug it. Do not disconnect the gas line or remove the gas control for this job.

Step 2: Close the cold water supply

Close the shut-off valve on the cold water pipe entering the heater. The inlet is marked on the top of the tank.

Step 3: Connect the hose and open a hot faucet

Thread the hose onto the drain valve near the bottom of the tank and run it to the drain. Then open a hot water faucet, preferably on a floor above the heater. This lets air into the tank so it drains instead of holding a vacuum.

Step 4: Drain the tank

Open the drain valve slowly. The water is often cloudy at first and may carry sand-like particles. How long the tank takes to empty depends on its size, the drain valve and the amount of sediment.

If the flow stops while the tank is still full, sediment has blocked the valve. Open the cold supply for a few seconds to push it through. Do not force a stiff plastic drain valve, because it can crack. A valve that will not seal afterward can be replaced with a brass boiler drain of the same thread size once the tank is empty.

Step 5: Flush the sediment

  1. With the drain valve open, open the cold supply for a short burst. The incoming water stirs the sediment and carries it out.
  2. Close the cold supply and let the tank drain.
  3. Repeat until the water from the hose is clear.

Step 6: Close the drain and refill

  1. Close the drain valve and remove the hose.
  2. Leave the hot faucet open and open the cold supply fully.
  3. Wait until water flows from the faucet in a steady stream with no sputtering. That means the tank is full and the air is out.
  4. Close the faucet, then check the drain valve for drips.

Step 7: Restore power or gas only when the tank is full

Electric: never switch the breaker on until the tank is full. Heating elements are designed to work under water. An element that is energized in air overheats and can burn out almost at once, which is called dry firing. If that happens, replacements are in water heater elements; match the voltage, wattage and mounting style on the old element. Replacing an element is electrical work, so use a plumber or electrician unless you are qualified to do it.

Gas: turn the control back to ON and to your normal temperature setting. If the pilot went out, relight it by following the lighting instructions on the heater's label exactly. Plug in the blower or control if you unplugged it. Allow time for the tank to reheat.

What about the T&P relief valve?

The temperature and pressure (T&P) relief valve on the top or side of the tank opens if the temperature or pressure becomes dangerous. Three rules apply:

  • Do not use it to vent the tank while draining. A hot faucet does the same job, and an old valve that is lifted may not reseat.
  • If you test it as the manufacturer recommends, stand clear of the discharge pipe. The water is scalding.
  • Never cap, plug or remove the valve or its discharge pipe. A valve that drips or will not reseat must be replaced with one that matches the pressure and BTU/h ratings on the heater's label. See relief valves.

A relief valve that discharges on its own often indicates excess pressure from thermal expansion, which a water heater expansion tank is designed to absorb. Have a plumber confirm the cause.

What else should you check while you are there?

  • Anode rod. The anode corrodes in place of the steel tank. If it is worn down to its core wire, replace it. See dip tubes and anode rods.
  • Leaks. Water from a fitting or valve can be repaired. Water from the tank shell itself means the heater needs replacing.

When to call a professional

  • You smell gas, or the pilot or burner will not relight normally after the flush.
  • The drain valve is blocked or will not close, and you are not able to replace it.
  • The T&P relief valve leaks, discharges or needs replacing.
  • The tank itself leaks, or still rumbles after a thorough flush.
  • You are not comfortable working around a 240 V circuit or a gas control.

If the tank is leaking or past its service life, compare replacements in residential gas tank water heaters, and see what size water heater you need.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need to turn off the water heater to flush it?

Yes. An electric element that is powered without water burns out, and a gas burner must not fire into an empty tank.

Does this apply to tankless water heaters?

No. Tankless heaters are descaled by circulating a cleaning solution through service valves, following the manufacturer's procedure.

To bleed a radiator, turn the heating off and let the system cool, open the bleed valve at the top of the radiator a quarter to half turn with a radiator key, let the air hiss out, and close the valve as soon as a steady stream of water appears. Then check the boiler pressure gauge and top the system up if it has dropped. If the boiler pressure is too high instead, the usual causes are a failed expansion tank, a fill valve that leaks through, or overfilling. This guide covers hot water (hydronic) systems only. Steam radiators have automatic air vents and are not bled this way.

How do you know a radiator needs bleeding?

  • The radiator is warm at the bottom and cool at the top.
  • You hear gurgling or the sound of running water in radiators or baseboard.
  • Upper-floor radiators heat poorly while lower ones are hot.

A radiator that is cold all over usually has a different problem: a closed radiator valve, a stuck zone valve or a circulator that is not running.

What you need

  • A radiator key, such as the Pasco radiator valve key, or a flat screwdriver for slotted vents
  • A rag and a small container
  • A boiler pressure gauge you can read.

How to bleed a radiator, step by step

  1. Find the cold spots. Run the heating until the radiators are warm and note which ones are cool at the top.
  2. Turn the heating off. Set the thermostat down so the circulator stops, and let the radiators cool until they are comfortable to touch. Water in a hot system can scald.
  3. Read the boiler pressure. Note the gauge reading. The system needs positive pressure to push the air out.
  4. Start on the lowest floor and work upward.
  5. Find the bleed valve. It is a small fitting near the top of the radiator, at one end.
  6. Open it slowly. Hold the rag and container under the vent and turn the key counterclockwise a quarter to half turn. Air will hiss out. Do not unscrew the stem completely.
  7. Close it when water flows. When water comes out in a steady stream with no sputtering, close the vent snugly. Do not overtighten.
  8. Repeat on every radiator with a vent.
  9. Check the pressure again and top up if needed (see below). Turn the heating on and confirm the radiators heat evenly.

A bleed valve that is corroded or drips after closing should be replaced. A coin-operated vent such as the Taco 417-3 coin vent (1/8 in. NPT) is a common replacement. Check the thread size first. The radiator must be isolated or the system drained below that level before a vent is unscrewed.

How do you bleed baseboard heat?

Most fin-tube baseboard has no bleed valve on each section. Some systems have a manual vent on an elbow under the end cover; if yours does, bleed it like a radiator. Otherwise air is removed by purging each zone with fresh water through a purge valve near the boiler: the zone's shut-off is closed, a hose is connected to the purge valve, and the fill valve's fast-fill lever pushes water through the loop until the hose runs free of air. The boiler must be off and cool, and the pressure gauge has to be watched throughout so it stays well below the relief valve setting. If you are not familiar with the valves on your boiler, have a heating technician purge it.

Can you stop bleeding by hand?

Automatic air vents release air on their own at high points and on air separators. A float inside opens the vent when air collects and closes it when water returns. An example is the Taco 400-4 Hy-Vent (1/8 in. NPT). For a system that collects air repeatedly, an air separator on the boiler supply removes dissolved air as the water heats. Browse all air vents.

What should boiler pressure be?

ConditionTypical readingMeaning
Cold systemAbout 12 psiTypical fill pressure for a one or two story house. Taco's instruction sheet gives 12 psi as the factory setting of its 329 fill valve.
Hot systemRises several psi above the cold readingNormal expansion
Approaching the relief valve settingToo highThe set pressure is stamped on the relief valve tag. On residential hot water boilers it is commonly 30 psi.
Well below the normal cold readingToo lowUpper radiators may not fill, and air can be drawn in

These are general figures. Fill pressure depends on the height of the system: each foot of height above the gauge needs 0.43 psi, plus a few psi at the top. Use the range in your boiler manual.

How do you top up boiler pressure after bleeding?

  1. Check that the valve on the cold water feed to the boiler is open. An automatic fill valve, such as the Taco 329-3 or the Resideo FM911/U combination fill valve and backflow preventer, brings the system back to its set pressure on its own.
  2. If the pressure is still low, lift the fast-fill lever briefly while watching the gauge, and release it at the normal cold pressure.
  3. On a combi boiler, use the built-in fill device as described in its manual. See the combi boiler guide.

A system that needs topping up often has a leak. Find it, because fresh water brings in more dissolved air and minerals.

Why is boiler pressure too high?

1. Failed or waterlogged expansion tank

The expansion tank gives heated water room to expand. A diaphragm separates system water from an air charge. When the air charge is lost or the diaphragm fails, the tank fills with water and the pressure climbs every time the boiler heats, then falls when it cools. This is the most common cause.

  • Check: press the air valve on the tank briefly. Water coming out means the diaphragm has failed and the tank must be replaced.
  • Pre-charge: the air charge is checked with the tank isolated from the system and drained of pressure, and is set to the system's cold fill pressure, per the tank manufacturer's instructions.
  • Replacement: size the tank by system volume and temperature. The Amtrol EX-15 Extrol is one residential example. See heating expansion tanks and what an expansion tank does.

2. Fill valve leaking through

If the pressure creeps up while the boiler is cold, the fill valve may be passing water from the house supply. Close the feed valve and watch the gauge for several hours. If the rise stops, have the fill valve repaired or replaced. Reopen the feed valve when the test is over, because the boiler should not be left without its water supply.

3. Overfilling

Holding the fast-fill lever too long leaves too much water in the system. With the system cold, drain a small amount from a boiler drain until the gauge shows the normal cold pressure.

4. Leak in an indirect water heater coil or tankless coil

Domestic water at house pressure can leak through a failed coil into the boiler loop. If the pressure rises with the feed valve closed, have the coil tested.

When to call a professional

  • The relief valve discharges. The system reached the valve's set pressure or the valve has failed. Turn the boiler off and have the cause found. Never plug or cap the valve or its discharge pipe, and never fit a relief valve with a higher pressure rating than the boiler's maximum working pressure. Replacement relief valves must match the boiler's pressure and BTU/h capacity.
  • The pressure keeps rising or falling after the checks above.
  • The expansion tank, fill valve or a radiator valve needs replacing and the system must be drained.
  • You have a steam system, or you are not sure which type you have.
  • The gauge reads zero, or does not move between cold and hot. The gauge may have failed.

Frequently asked questions

Should the heating be on or off when bleeding radiators?

Off, with the circulator stopped and the radiators cooled. Run it first only to find the cold spots.

Why does boiler pressure rise when the heating is on?

Water expands as it heats, so a rise of a few psi is normal. A rise toward the relief valve setting usually means the expansion tank has lost its air charge or failed.

Why does my boiler keep losing pressure?

Bleeding releases some pressure, which is normal. Continued loss means a leak or a dripping relief valve.

To connect PEX to copper, use a transition fitting made for both materials. There are three common ways: solder a sweat x PEX adapter onto the copper and crimp, clamp or expand the PEX onto its barb; push both pipes into a push-to-connect coupling; or join a threaded copper adapter to a threaded PEX adapter. PEX and copper tube of the same nominal size have the same outside diameter, so 1/2 in. PEX connects to 1/2 in. copper and 3/4 in. to 3/4 in. The right method depends on the tools you have and whether an open flame is safe where you are working.

Which method should you use?

MethodToolsGood forWatch for
Sweat x PEX adapterTorch, lead-free solder, flux, PEX crimp, clamp or expansion toolPermanent joints, lowest fitting costOpen flame. Solder before the PEX is attached.
Push-to-connect couplingTube cutter, deburring and depth toolRepairs, tight spaces, no flamePipe ends must be round, clean and deburred. Check the listing for concealed or buried use.
Threaded adaptersTorch or press tool for the copper side, wrenches, PEX toolJoints you may need to take apart, valves and equipment connectionsThread sealant rated for potable water. Do not overtighten.
Press x PEX adapterCopper press tool, PEX toolNo flame, fast on wet linesFittings and jaws from the same press system

Check the pipe sizes and the PEX type first

  • Copper: Types K, L and M have the same outside diameter for a given nominal size. According to the Copper Development Association, the outside diameter is 1/8 in. larger than the nominal size: 1/2 in. copper tube measures 5/8 in. outside, and 3/4 in. measures 7/8 in.
  • PEX: read the print line on the tubing. It gives the size, the type (PEX-A, PEX-B or PEX-C) and the fitting standards the tubing is listed for, such as ASTM F1807, F2159 or F1960.

The fitting system has to match the tubing. Crimp and clamp fittings (F1807 and F2159) work on any PEX listed for them. Cold expansion fittings (F1960) are for tubing listed to F1960, which is mainly PEX-A. See PEX-A vs PEX-B for the differences.

Before you cut

  • Shut off the water at the main or the nearest stop, open a faucet below the work to drain the line, and have a bucket ready.
  • Check where the pipe goes. Do not use PEX within the distance from a water heater or flue that the tubing manufacturer and your plumbing code prohibit. The Uniform Plumbing Code does not allow PEX within the first 18 inches of piping connected to a water heater. Check the code edition your jurisdiction has adopted.
  • In many homes the metal water piping is bonded to the electrical system. Replacing a section of copper with PEX breaks that path. See "When to call a professional" below.

Method 1: Sweat (solder) adapter

A sweat adapter has a copper socket or a fitting-size copper end on one side and a PEX barb or expansion end on the other.

  1. Cut the copper square with a tubing cutter. Deburr it, then clean the pipe end and the fitting socket with abrasive cloth or a fitting brush until bright.
  2. Solder the adapter with no PEX attached. Apply flux, assemble, heat the fitting evenly and feed lead-free solder into the joint. The line must be empty: a joint with water in it will not reach soldering temperature.
  3. Let the joint cool completely. Heat travels along copper and will damage PEX that is attached too soon.
  4. Attach the PEX. Cut the tubing square. For crimp or clamp: slide the ring on, push the tubing fully onto the barb, position the ring 1/8 to 1/4 in. from the end of the tubing, as ASTM F1807 and the fitting instructions specify, and compress it with the tool. Check copper crimp rings with a go/no-go gauge. For expansion: expand the tubing and ring, push onto the fitting to the shoulder and let it shrink.
  5. Turn the water on slowly and check for leaks.

Where possible, solder the adapter to a short length of copper at a bench, then join that piece to the existing pipe with a coupling. This keeps the flame away from framing. When soldering in place, use a heat shield, keep an extinguisher within reach and check for smoldering afterward. Fittings are in copper sweat fittings and PEX crimp fittings (F1807).

Method 2: Push-to-connect fitting

A push-to-connect coupling holds each pipe with a stainless steel grab ring and seals it with an O-ring. Fittings certified to ASSE 1061 are made for copper, PEX and CPVC of copper tube size.

  1. Cut both pipes square. Use a tubing cutter on copper and a PEX cutter on PEX.
  2. Deburr and clean the copper. A burr or sharp edge can cut the O-ring. The sealing area must be free of scratches, solder and flat spots.
  3. Check for the tube stiffener. PEX needs a stiffener inside the tube end. Many brass push fittings have one built in. If not, fit one as the instructions require.
  4. Mark the insertion depth on each pipe using the manufacturer's depth gauge.
  5. Push each pipe in to the mark, then turn the water on and check for leaks.

Whether a push fitting may be concealed in a wall or buried depends on its listing and your local code, so check both. Browse push fittings.

Method 3: Threaded or press transition

Threaded: solder or press a male or female threaded adapter onto the copper, then screw on the matching PEX adapter (crimp, clamp or expansion x thread). Apply PTFE tape or pipe sealant rated for potable water to the male threads. Make the soldered joint first and let it cool before threading on a PEX adapter that already has tubing attached.

Press: with a copper press tool, a press x PEX adapter joins the two without flame and works on a line that will not drain fully. The copper must be clean, round and deburred, and marked for insertion depth.

For PEX-A expansion systems, see F1960 expansion fittings. Cutters, crimpers and clamp tools are in PEX tools, and tubing is in PEX pipe and tubing.

What mistakes cause leaks?

  • Soldering with the PEX attached, or attaching it before the joint has cooled.
  • Skipping the deburring. Burrs cut O-rings in push fittings.
  • Mixing fitting systems. Use rings and fittings listed for the tubing. Do not use F1960 expansion fittings on tubing that is not listed for F1960.
  • Tubing not fully inserted, or a crimp ring placed too close to or too far from the end.
  • No support. Fasten both the copper and the PEX near the transition so the fitting does not carry the weight or movement of the pipe.
  • Joining dissimilar metals directly. PEX adapters are brass or copper and are compatible with copper tube. Galvanized steel is a different case and needs a dielectric fitting.

When to call a professional

  • Electrical bonding. If the copper you are cutting is near the water meter or main shut-off, or a ground clamp is attached to the piping, have an electrician check whether a bonding jumper is required before the copper path is interrupted.
  • Water heater connections, especially on gas heaters, where clearances from the flue apply.
  • Soldering inside walls or near insulation if you have not soldered before. A press or push fitting, or a plumber, avoids the fire risk.
  • Work that needs a permit. Repiping and new branch lines usually do. Pressure test before closing walls.
  • Hydronic heating lines. These need oxygen-barrier PEX and components rated for the system temperature.

Frequently asked questions

Can you connect PEX directly to copper?

Yes, with a transition fitting: a sweat x PEX adapter, a push-to-connect coupling, or threaded or press adapters. PEX cannot be soldered or glued.

Is 1/2 in. PEX the same size as 1/2 in. copper?

The outside diameter is the same, 5/8 in., because both are copper tube size. The PEX wall is thicker, so its inside diameter is smaller.

Can PEX-A and PEX-B use the same copper adapters?

Crimp and clamp adapters fit any PEX listed for F1807 or F2159. Expansion adapters fit only tubing listed for F1960.
