PEX-A and PEX-B are both cross-linked polyethylene water tubing made to the same standard (ASTM F876) with the same pressure ratings. The difference is how they are cross-linked, and that changes how they handle. PEX-A is more flexible, can be joined with cold expansion fittings (ASTM F1960) and can be repaired with a heat gun if it kinks. PEX-B is stiffer and is joined with crimp or clamp fittings. The letters are not quality grades: A, B and C only identify the manufacturing method.

PEX-A vs PEX-B: quick comparison

 PEX-APEX-B
Cross-linking methodPeroxide (Engel), during extrusionSilane (moisture cure), after extrusion
FlexibilityMore flexible, tighter bend radiusStiffer, more coil memory
Usual fitting systemF1960 cold expansion. Also crimp or clamp if the tubing is listed for it.Crimp or clamp (F1807 or F2159 fittings)
ToolsExpansion toolCrimp or clamp tool
Kink repairHeat gun, following the manufacturer's procedureCut out the kink and install a coupling
Pressure rating (ASTM F876)The same for both types in the same size and wall thickness. The ratings are printed on the tubing.

What do the letters A, B and C mean?

Plain polyethylene softens with heat. Cross-linking bonds its long molecules into a network, which gives PEX its resistance to heat, pressure and creep. The letter tells you which process made those bonds:

  • PEX-A (peroxide or Engel method): peroxide is mixed into the polyethylene and the cross-linking takes place while the material is hot, during extrusion.
  • PEX-B (silane method): a silane compound is grafted onto the polyethylene, the tubing is extruded, and cross-linking is completed afterward with heat and moisture.
  • PEX-C (irradiation method): the extruded tubing is cross-linked with an electron beam. It is joined with crimp or clamp fittings.

ASTM F876 requires every PEX tube, whatever the method, to meet a minimum degree of cross-linking and to pass the same pressure, temperature and chlorine resistance tests. A higher degree of cross-linking does not mean a higher pressure rating.

Which is more flexible?

PEX-A. It uncoils more easily, bends tighter and is easier to work in cold weather and tight framing. Tighter bends mean fewer elbows. PEX-B holds more of its coil shape, needs a larger bend radius and uses bend supports or elbow fittings more often. Its stiffness can be an advantage on long straight runs.

The minimum bend radius is set by the tubing manufacturer. Bending tighter than that can kink the tubing.

Which fittings work with PEX-A and PEX-B?

The fitting system is the most practical difference, because it decides which tool you need.

ConnectionStandardHow it worksTubing
Cold expansion with PEX ringASTM F1960The tool expands the tube end and ring, the fitting is inserted, and the tube shrinks back onto itTubing listed for F1960, mainly PEX-A
Copper crimp ringASTM F1807 (metal insert), F2159 (plastic insert)A copper ring is compressed over the tube and insert fittingPEX-B, PEX-C, and PEX-A listed for it
Stainless clamp (cinch) ringASTM F2098 rings on F1807 or F2159 fittingsA stainless band is cinched over the tube and insert fittingPEX-B, PEX-C, and PEX-A listed for it
Push-to-connectASSE 1061The tube pushes into a fitting with a grab ring and O-ringAny type the fitting is listed for

Expansion fittings (F1960)

Expansion joints depend on the tubing shrinking back to its original size, which PEX-A does reliably. Because the tube is stretched over the fitting instead of the fitting being inserted into an unstretched tube, an F1960 fitting has a larger bore than an insert fitting of the same nominal size and restricts flow less. In cold conditions the joint takes longer to shrink, so wait before pressure testing.

Use F1960 fittings only on tubing whose print line lists F1960. Some manufacturers make expansion-capable PEX-B with their own rings and fittings. Do not mix components between systems unless the manufacturers list them together. See F1960 expansion fittings and PEX expansion tools.

Crimp and clamp fittings (F1807, F2159)

Crimp and clamp fittings work on PEX-B and PEX-C and on PEX-A that is listed for them. Crimp tools are sized to the ring and each joint is checked with a go/no-go gauge. Clamp tools usually cover several sizes with one tool. See PEX crimp fittings (F1807), all PEX fittings and PEX tools.

Can a kink in PEX be repaired?

  • PEX-A: manufacturers of PEX-A allow a kink to be repaired by warming the section evenly with a heat gun until the tubing returns to its round shape. Follow the manufacturer's procedure, never use an open flame, and do not repair tubing that is under pressure.
  • PEX-B: a kink cannot be heat-repaired. Cut it out and install a coupling.

How do tools and fittings affect the choice?

  • Tools: an expansion system needs an expansion tool, and a crimp or clamp system needs a crimp or clamp tool. For a small repair, the tool you already own often decides the choice.
  • Whole-house work: PEX-A's flexibility reduces the number of fittings needed on a repipe.

What applies to both types?

  • Read the print line. It lists the standards, pressure ratings and fitting systems the tubing is certified for. Potable water tubing carries NSF/ANSI/CAN 61.
  • Sunlight. PEX is not for permanent outdoor exposure. Each product has a maximum UV exposure time, so store it covered.
  • Heat. Keep PEX away from flues and recessed lights and follow the code and manufacturer's minimum distance at water heater connections.
  • Heating systems. Hydronic heating with ferrous components needs PEX with an oxygen barrier. Standard potable PEX of either type does not have one.
  • Freezing. PEX tolerates freezing better than rigid pipe but can still split, and fittings can fail. Protect lines in unheated spaces.

Which should you choose?

  • Choose PEX-A for a repipe or a large project, when you want expansion fittings and the tightest bends, or when you already own an expansion tool.
  • Choose PEX-B for repairs and smaller projects, or when you already own a crimp or clamp tool.
  • Either way, stay with one connection system for the whole job and use tubing, fittings and rings that are listed together.

Browse PEX pipe and tubing. To join new PEX to existing copper, see how to connect PEX to copper.

When to call a professional

  • A whole-house repipe or new supply lines. These usually need a permit, a pressure test and an inspection before walls are closed.
  • Connections at a water heater or boiler.
  • Replacing copper that is part of the electrical bonding path. An electrician should check whether a bonding jumper is needed.
  • Any installation where you cannot confirm from the print line that the tubing and fittings are listed together.

Frequently asked questions

Is PEX-A better than PEX-B?

Not in rating. Both meet ASTM F876 and carry the same pressure ratings. PEX-A is easier to bend and allows expansion fittings. PEX-B is stiffer and uses crimp or clamp fittings.

Can I use crimp rings on PEX-A?

Yes, if the tubing's print line lists ASTM F1807 or F2159.

Can I use expansion fittings on PEX-B?

Only on PEX-B that its manufacturer lists for F1960 expansion, with the rings that manufacturer specifies. Standard PEX-B is not suitable.

Can PEX-A and PEX-B be joined together?

Yes, with a coupling whose fitting system is listed for both tubes, such as a crimp or push-to-connect coupling.

Most zone valve replacements do not require replacing the whole valve. On Taco 570 series and Honeywell V8043 zone valves, the part that usually fails is the power head (actuator), and it can be changed without draining the system or cutting pipe. Replace the head with the same brand, series and voltage, and wire the new one exactly like the old one. The full valve needs replacing only when the body leaks, is seized, or you are changing brand or pipe connection. This guide explains how to tell which part has failed, how Taco and Honeywell (Resideo) valves differ, and what each replacement involves.

Is the zone valve the problem?

SymptomLikely causePart to replace
One zone stays cold, others heatHead not opening the valve, or no 24 V reaching itPower head, after confirming voltage at the head
One zone overheats with its thermostat satisfiedValve stuck open, or debris on the seatPower head first. Full valve if the body does not close.
Zone valve opens but the boiler or circulator does not startFailed end switchPower head
Water at the valve stem or bodyStem seal or body leakFull valve
All zones coldNot a zone valve: check the boiler, circulator, transformer and aquastatNone

Both brands have a manual opening lever on the valve. If the lever moves the valve open and the zone then heats, the body is working and the head or its wiring is at fault.

How does a zone valve work?

A zone valve is an electrically operated valve on the piping of one heating zone. When that zone's thermostat calls for heat, 24 VAC from a transformer powers the actuator and the valve opens. When the valve is fully open, an end switch inside the head closes and signals the boiler and circulator to run. When the thermostat is satisfied, power is removed and the valve closes.

The valve has two parts: the brass body, which is soldered, threaded or pressed into the piping, and the power head, which holds the motor and end switch.

Taco vs Honeywell zone valves: what is the difference?

 Taco 570 seriesHoneywell V8043
ActuatorHeat motor: a heated element expands and pushes the valve openElectric motor opens the valve, a spring closes it
OpeningGradual. A delay after the thermostat calls is normal.Faster
Voltage24 VAC24 VAC (V8043). The V4043 is the 120 V version.
WiringThree screw terminals. The motor and end switch connections are shown on Taco's wiring diagram.Lead wires or a terminal block, depending on the model. The V8043E1012 has lead wires.
Head replaceable with the system fullYesYes, with the head specified for that valve

Neither design is better in every system. The practical rule is to replace like with like, so the wiring, transformer load and piping stay the same. Heads are not interchangeable between brands, and not always between series of the same brand: Taco Zone Sentry valves, for example, do not use 570 series heads.

Which wiring type do you have?

  • Two-wire, no end switch: the thermostat circuit powers the actuator and nothing else. Used where a zone control panel starts the boiler and circulator.
  • Three-wire (Taco 570): three terminals serve both the motor and the end switch.
  • Four-wire (Honeywell V8043 models with an end switch): two motor connections and two end switch connections.

Because the two brands arrange the motor and end switch connections differently, they cannot be swapped wire for wire. Converting between them means rewiring to the new valve's diagram and checking that the transformer can carry the load of all the valves.

Which models are common?

  • Taco 571-2: the Taco 571-2 is a 3/4 in. sweat, two-way heat motor zone valve. The 570 family covers other pipe sizes.
  • Taco 555-050RP: the 555-050RP power unit is a Taco replacement power head. Confirm on Taco's replacement parts list that it fits your valve model before ordering.
  • Honeywell V8043E1012: the V8043E1012/U is a 24 VAC, 3/4 in. sweat, normally closed valve with 18 in. lead wires.
  • Honeywell V8044: the three-way diverting version of the V8043.

Honeywell Home zone valves are now made by Resideo, so either name may be on the label. Browse Taco zone valves, Honeywell zone valves and zone valve replacement heads.

How to replace a zone valve power head

This is low-voltage work with the system left full. It still requires the power to be off, because zone valve wiring connects to boiler controls.

  1. Copy the full model number from the head and the valve body, and order the head listed for that valve.
  2. Turn off power to the boiler and to the zone valve transformer or zone control.
  3. Photograph the wiring and label each wire.
  4. Disconnect the wires.
  5. Remove the head from the body as the manufacturer's instructions describe for that model. Do not loosen the body or its bonnet: the system is under pressure.
  6. Fit the new head and check that it is fully seated and latched.
  7. Reconnect the wires to the same terminals or lead colors, following the diagram supplied with the head.
  8. Restore power and raise the zone thermostat. Confirm that the valve opens, the end switch starts the boiler or circulator, and the zone heats. Then lower the thermostat and confirm that the valve closes and the zone cools.

When does the whole valve need replacing?

  • The body or stem leaks.
  • The valve stays stuck open or closed with a working head.
  • You are changing brand, pipe size or connection type, or the head for that valve is no longer made.

Replacing the body means isolating or draining the zone, removing the old valve, soldering, threading or pressing in the new one with the flow arrow in the right direction, then refilling, purging air and checking the system pressure. Follow the manufacturer's soldering instructions for a sweat body, which may require the head to be removed first, so heat does not damage the valve. After refilling, see how to bleed a radiator and check boiler pressure.

What to confirm before you order

  • Brand, series and full model number of the head and the body
  • Voltage: 24 VAC or 120 V. Never fit a 24 V head on a 120 V circuit, or the reverse.
  • Normally closed or normally open
  • End switch or no end switch, and terminal block or lead wires
  • For a full valve: pipe size, connection type (sweat, threaded, flare or press) and two-way or three-way

When to call a professional

  • Full valve replacement, unless you are experienced with soldering and with draining, refilling and purging a hydronic system.
  • Any 120 V zone valve (V4043, V4044) or line voltage wiring.
  • A transformer or zone control that keeps failing, or a new head that burns out, which points to a wiring fault or an overloaded transformer.
  • Changing brands, where the end switch wiring to the boiler has to be redesigned.
  • The boiler does not fire after the repair. Do not jumper boiler controls or limits to test it.
  • The relief valve discharges or the pressure will not stabilize after refilling.

Frequently asked questions

Can I replace a Taco zone valve with a Honeywell?

Yes, but it is a full valve replacement and a rewiring job, because the end switch arrangements differ. Replacing with the same brand is simpler.

Do I have to drain the system to replace a zone valve head?

Usually not. On Taco 570 valves and on Honeywell V8043 valves with a removable head, the head comes off the body with the system full. Check the instructions for your model.

Why does a Taco zone valve take time to open?

Its heat motor has to warm up before it moves the valve. The delay is normal for that design.
